articleTitle: The defence fixed telecommunications system-the first steps
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: Summary form only given. The author looks at the present developments by describing how a formal grouping of scientific and procurement agencies, representing all three arms, together with a strong standardisation presence, is drawing up the technical interface parameters which will allow existing, and foreseen systems, to interwork and ultimately to federate into one system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Efficient implementation of X.25 on narrowband packet radio systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: In order to maintain the maximum flexibility in the deployment of components of CIS (command, control and intelligence) systems and to simplify the design, implementation and deployment of the gateways, a common network interface is required. With the NATO policy of applying ISO based protocols (with military enhancements) wherever possible, this suggests the X.25 series of protocols for the bottom three layers of the OSI model. The author describes a combination of communications protocols with signal processing techniques designed to provide data communications in the far forward tactical environment by applying packet switching techniques to conventional combat net radio.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Functional profiles for military message handling
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The authors describe the implementation and analysis of a number of message handling systems. These range from systems which were defined before functional profiles came into use, through systems where functional profiles were added following the production of an operational requirement using a traditional approach, to procurements written around functional profiles. They cover the advantages and disadvantages for both the procurer and the supplier in using functional profiles.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparison of civil and military requirements for C31S systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The author discusses the civil and military applications of C3IS systems with respect to following comparisons: user/system requirements, support requirements including engineering standards, engineering solutions in the use of commercial and military products and their ownership costs. A generalised view of the main functional subsystems for a C3IS command and control system is also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Is there a role for OSI security management in military networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The author demonstrates that the OSI security management has a role within military networks, since they usually employ a large number and variety of security mechanisms. OSI security management is designed to provide a common method for managing OSI security mechanisms. OSI Management generally is intended to readily facilitate private management extensions to the standards by, wherever possible, separating the information to be communicated from the protocol itself. This point is as true for security management as it is for configuration or fault management. The flexibility of an object oriented management methodology means that the military can adopt standard protocols and indeed standard managed objects, which can be turned into specific military managed objects by simply adding new attributes or modifying existing attributes. In order that military requirements are addressed, the military however must be prepared to contribute to the standardization process.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The author describes how the NATO's interest in the OSI programme first became apparent in order to achieve greater interoperability between digital communication systems and the setting up of NIMP (NATO interoperability management plan) for the adoption of OSI. He also describes a SANTIS (single-architecture NATO technical interface standard) which is currently composed of a family of STANAGs (standardisation agreements). The enhancements needed to meet the military requirements in the current ISO/CCITT based standards are described in detail.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of C.C.I.T.T. No 7 signalling to support military enhancements
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The author describes one particular but important enhancement needed to GPT's equipment to meet the needs of an armed forces customer, being the need to signal information specific to these special military requirements across the network. He describes the investigation of signalling system standards available at the time of inception of the project, the enhancements made to CCITT No. 7 common channel signalling to meet the customers needs, and pertinent practical information about the implementation and use of specially enhanced signalling systems. The backbone of this system is an extensive network of PABXs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The author describes the advantages and disadvantages in using satellite-based military communication systems compared to terrestrial networks. The topics covered are: areas of use (tactical and strategic), threats to SATCOMS (physical and electronic), methods to counter threats, present advantages/disadvantages of EHF frequency band and technology trends in general.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Military Communications - The Trend Towards Civil Standards
abstract: The author addresses some of the major implications of the CCITT X.400 1988 recommendations on the procurement of message handling systems for the military. He gives an overview of the facilities of X.400(88), analyses the civil facilities from the military view points and illustrates by using X.400 as an example, how civil standards can be tailored to meet military requirements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
